title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

infographic.key_insight: GBClaw links agentic AI workflows with atomistic simulations to reveal how defect hierarchies and metastable structures influence grain-boundary sliding resistance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding grain-boundary deformation mechanisms can inform efforts to control interfacial strength in polycrystalline materials.
method: Coordinate LLM-based specialized agents through an orchestrator, domain tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory.
Dynamically replan simulations and mechanistic analyses as results emerge.
Compare sliding with and without secondary grain-boundary misfit dislocations, then investigate anomalies through researcher-guided calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel, GBClaw identified diverse deformation modes and substantial shear-strength differences associated with secondary misfit dislocations.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the studied nickel boundaries, and resolving an anomalously high shear resistance required researcher-guided follow-up.
infographic.paper_title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery

title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films
authors: K. Starkey, L. Kahle, M. Christensen, V. Eyert, A. El-Azab, C. B. Geller
abstract: A first-principles-informed multiscale modeling approach is reported for oxide formation during corrosion of zirconium. The present simulations reproduce the columnar corrosion film microstructure and grain size distribution seen in micrographs of oxidized Zr surfaces. This structural feature emerges from a hexagonal ZrO layer adjacent to the $α$-Zr/ZrO$_{2-x}$ interface, which is dynamically stabilized by continuous heterogeneous grain nucleation and grain boundary mass diffusion. This ZrO layer is identified as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier and a potential contributor to sub-parabolic pretransition corrosion kinetics. The simulations also reproduce the undulatory nature of the metal/oxide interface, leading to regions with tensile stress components capable of nucleating cracks, despite the overall state of compressive hydrostatic stress within the oxide film. First principles density functional theory (DFT) computations of fundamental ZrO$_x$ properties were combined with molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned potential based on a DFT training set to provide extensive input to an advanced phase field model for oxide formation and its microstructure, as implemented in the new MedeA PhaseField module. The phase field simulations reported herein incorporated computed stoichiometry-dependent thermochemical data, anisotropic elastic properties, interface energies, bulk and grain boundary mass transport processes, multiphase heterogeneous grain nucleation, and strain energy-dependent phase stabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Multiscale simulations identify a dynamically stabilized hexagonal ZrO interlayer that helps explain columnar oxide growth and acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier during zirconium corrosion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting oxide microstructure, oxygen transport barriers, and local tensile stresses could inform assessments of zirconium corrosion and crack initiation.
method: Compute ZrOₓ properties using first-principles density functional theory.
Use molecular dynamics with a DFT-trained machine-learned potential to supply additional material inputs.
Model oxide evolution with multiphase phase fields coupling nucleation, diffusion, elasticity, and phase stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations reproduce columnar oxide morphology and grain size distributions seen in micrographs, as well as an undulating metal/oxide interface.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation errors or demonstrated prediction of corrosion rates; the ZrO layer’s contribution to sub-parabolic kinetics remains tentative.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films

title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction
authors: Adam Zheng, April Zheng, Sheng Ran
abstract: AI/ML models are useful for the prediction of materials' properties. Recently, there has been great progress in developing Neural Network models to predict the properties of solids, molecules, and crystals, avoiding expensive and time-consuming laboratory testing. This study presents a novel AI/ML-based multi-modal approach to predict material magnetic ordering using material crystal structure information as input to a Graph Neural Network model (GNN) and semantic text descriptions of the material's properties and structure as input to a Large Language Model (LLM), before performing information fusion of the GNN and LLM outputs to predict material magnetic ordering in four classes (Non-magnetic, Ferromagnetic, Antiferromagnetic, Ferrimagnetic). The model is trained, validated, and tested on a dataset which is a combination of Materials Project dataset, Magndata dataset, and a set of uranium compounds with magnetic ordering determined in laboratory testing, with an 80/10/10 (training/validation/testing) data split. The proposed GNN and LLM multi-modal approach achieves better overall accuracy than both the standalone GNN and LLM approaches with three fusion strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Combining crystal-structure GNN outputs with an LLM text branch improves overall magnetic-ordering classification accuracy over either standalone model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support computational screening of magnetic materials before costly laboratory characterization.
method: Encode material crystal structures with a graph neural network.
Process semantic descriptions of material properties and structure with a large language model.
Fuse outputs using three strategies to classify non-magnetic, ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or ferrimagnetic ordering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses combined Materials Project, Magndata, and laboratory-characterized uranium-compound data with an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split; the abstract reports improved overall accuracy but gives no numerical scores.
infographic.watch_item: Text descriptions should be checked for magnetic-label leakage before interpreting the multimodal accuracy gains.
infographic.paper_title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction

title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
authors: Joseph Hart, Samuel G. H. Brookes, Fabian L. Thiemann, Christoph Schran
abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.

infographic.key_insight: Low DFT energy and force errors do not guarantee reliable disordered-carbon simulations; MACE-MH-1 was the most consistently robust foundation MLIP tested.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Application-specific validation can help engineers select reliable MLIPs for nanoporous carbon simulations, including more realistic oxygen- and hydrogen-containing structures.
method: Screen six foundation MLIPs using DFT energy and force errors and binding curves.
Test four models with melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and structural analysis.
Evaluate pure and O/H-containing disordered carbons across phases, hybridisations and porous frameworks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories exposed failures missed by low DFT errors, while all four MD-tested models reproduced principal experimental and specialised-potential signatures of nanoporous carbon.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness is application-dependent: shared structural biases in OMAT-based models highlight training-coverage concerns despite differing architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons

title: Instability-driven segregation of V group transition metals on HEB$_2$ grain boundaries influencing enhanced mechanical properties
authors: Daniil Alekseev, Viktor S. Baidyshev, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: Five metals share a common sublattice in the (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B$_2$ (HEB$_2$). Most high-entropy materials are produced as polycrystalline materials in the form of sintered ceramics. The question of which metal species are located at grain boundaries is still unknown. Here, we calculated the grain-boundary energy $γ_{GB}$ of four types of boundaries in five binary diborides and HEB$_2$ using density functional theory (DFT). We analyzed the bonding at these boundaries using COHP and sampled cation segregation at six boundaries of HEB$_2$, ordered and general, using Monte Carlo / molecular dynamics with a MACE potential that was fine-tuned for this system. According to our results $γ_{GB}$ splits by group: the group V diborides NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$ form boundaries with about half the energy of the group IV at three of the four types of GBs, ranging from 0.8 to 2.7 compared to 2.5--4.8~J/m$^2$. COHP shows a significant difference at the Fermi level, namely the Me--B bonds of NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$ are antibonding at Fermi energy ($E_F$) in the bulk but bonding at the GB, while their integrated strength hardly changes. In HEB$_2$ the segregation follows a similar pattern: Nb and Ta are enriched at five of the six grain boundaries, including general boundaries, up to 23--35~at.\% at 2000~K, although the size of the atoms would favor Zr and Hf in the expanded sites. A segregated $Σ193$ grain boundary can withstand 26 against 20~GPa for a random boundary in tension at 300~K. The grain boundaries of HEB$_2$ are composed of group V metals, as suggested by the boundary energies of binaries compounds and their bonding at the Fermi level. Grain boundaries of the (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B$_2$ preferentially include Nb and Ta. This lowers the grain boundary energy and strengthens the boundaries. This consists of the lower boundary energy and changes Fermi level bonding in NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$.

infographic.key_insight: Nb and Ta preferentially segregate to grain boundaries in (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B₂, linking group V bonding behavior to lower boundary energies and stronger interfaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling grain-boundary chemistry could improve the mechanical performance of high-entropy diboride ceramics.
method: DFT calculations of four grain-boundary types in five binary diborides and HEB₂.
COHP analysis of metal–boron bonding at grain boundaries.
Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics sampling of six HEB₂ boundaries using a fine-tuned MACE potential.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nb and Ta enrichment reached 23–35 at.% at 2000 K across five of six boundaries; at 300 K, a segregated Σ193 boundary sustained 26 GPa in tension versus 20 GPa for a random boundary.
infographic.watch_item: These computational predictions require experimental validation, and the tensile-strength comparison concerns a single boundary type.
infographic.paper_title: Instability-driven segregation of V group transition metals on HEB$_2$ grain boundaries influencing enhanced mechanical properties

title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
authors: Ziqiao Meng, Rongsheng Chen, Zhi Zheng, Nikita Kazeev, Zhenkun Wang, Andrey Ustyuzhanin
abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

infographic.key_insight: CrystalAR unifies symmetry-template and crystal-structure generation in one autoregressive sequence, expressing continuous atomic positions through hierarchical discrete localization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a symmetry-preserving route to new crystal candidates and crystal structure prediction without retrieving symmetry templates from prior data.
method: Jointly generate Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures.
Refine symmetry-inequivalent site positions across discrete spatial resolution levels, jointly modeling sites within each level.
Use constraint-aware search over crystallographic templates and geometric realizations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong symmetry-template generation and competitive de novo generation and template-free crystal structure prediction, but provides no benchmark names or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical use should assess how spatial resolution and constraint-aware search affect geometric accuracy and computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation

title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations
authors: Ali Karatutlu, Timuçin Emre Tabaru, Umut Taylan, Zehra Gizem Mutlay, Doğukan Hazar Özbey, Okan Uslu
abstract: Silicon-on-insulator is mostly the main driving material system for the field of silicon photonics, including PICs, due to high index contrast and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes [1]. A recent example is silicon oxynitride-doped silicon [2] discovered recently by our group, offering to set a new position for the fields of silicon photonics with a precise control of refractive index from 2.1 to 2.5 together with the photosensitivity property at different wavelengths. In this study, we demonstrate that the synthesis of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be performed on a flexible substrate for the fabrication of Bragg gratings (BG) at low temperatures below 100 degrees Celsius that are emerging for advanced applications. Their use in preserving ultra-fast lasers inscribed micro-information has been demonstrated numerically and experimentally due to its multispectral reflection behaviour from the ultraviolet (UV) to the near-infrared (NIR) regions. The unique structural characteristics of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon were studied at the Si L, O K and N K edges using soft X-ray absorption studies. The quantum mechanical calculations provide the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, whereas the crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx was conducted using the particle swarm optimization method in combination with density functional theory (DFT).

infographic.key_insight: Silicon oxynitride-doped silicon films enable flexible, laser-inscribed Bragg gratings with UV-to-near-infrared reflection for authentication applications.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Synthesis below 100 °C and refractive-index control from 2.1 to 2.5 support flexible photonic structures for encoding optically readable micro-information.
method: Synthesize silicon oxynitride-doped silicon on flexible substrates and inscribe Bragg gratings using ultrafast lasers.
Probe local structure using soft X-ray absorption at the Si L, O K and N K edges.
Investigate formation mechanisms with quantum calculations and predict bulk Si3N4−xOx structures using particle swarm optimization coupled with DFT.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical and experimental demonstrations of micro-information preservation through multispectral reflection, but provides no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Bending durability and long-term optical stability are not established in the abstract and need validation for practical authentication.
infographic.paper_title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations

title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
authors: Reza T Batley, Sourav Saha
abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

infographic.key_insight: Rectified-flow generation paired with exact latent-space refinement enables concurrent design of printable bone-scaffold microstructures and their spatial placement to meet mechanical targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports highly porous, mechanically constrained implants and could extend to topology–microstructure co-design for metal additive manufacturing.
method: Generate periodic lattice unit cells with a conditional rectified-flow model.
Refine cells in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities.
Jointly optimize cell geometries and spatial assignments under mechanical and feature-size constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: All eight rabbit-benchmark refinements achieved under 1% maximum relative error across six target moduli; human femoral designs reached 63% cortical porosity with compliance within 2% of its constraint and 84% cancellous porosity with strain-energy deviations below 0.25%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational benchmarks, not physical fabrication or biological validation of the scaffolds.
infographic.paper_title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement

title: MOFFieldBench: A Machine Learning Benchmark for Continuous Electronic Fields in Metal-Organic Frameworks
authors: Zhaolin Hu, Hehe Fan, Chenhao Rao, Wangyihan Guo, Meng Xu, Qiwei Yang
abstract: Machine-learning models for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) predominantly rely on atomic structures, whereas electron-density (ED) and electrostatic-potential (ESP) fields remain underexplored as scalable learning representations. These continuous fields encode complementary spatial and electronic information relevant to structure-property relationships, particularly pore geometry and guest-framework interactions, but costly first-principles calculations, storage requirements and the scarcity of systematically aligned datasets limit their broader use. Here we introduce MOFFieldBench, a multimodal benchmark comprising approximately 46,000 MOFs with one-to-one aligned crystallographic structures, ED fields and ESP fields. A unified workflow integrates field generation, error-controlled compression and sparse point-cloud representation, supporting field reconstruction, prediction of 13 material properties, multimodal property prediction and pairwise cross-modal retrieval. ED and ESP provide competitive representations for pore geometry, adsorption and separation properties. Multimodal fusion improves several prediction tasks relative to the best unimodal reference, supporting complementary predictive roles for atomic structures and electronic fields. Learned ED reconstruction closely approximates first-principles reference densities, while predicted-density initialization reduces self-consistent-field calculation time by 13.59\% on average in paired tests. These results support electronic fields as practical, informative learning modalities and establish MOFFieldBench as a resource for studying representation choice, multimodal learning and electronic-field-driven MOF modelling.

infographic.key_insight: MOFFieldBench shows that electron-density and electrostatic-potential fields complement atomic structures for machine-learning prediction of metal-organic framework properties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Electronic-field representations can support pore, adsorption and separation modelling, while predicted electron densities can accelerate first-principles calculations.
method: Align crystallographic structures, electron-density fields and electrostatic-potential fields for approximately 46,000 MOFs.
Combine field generation, error-controlled compression and sparse point-cloud representations.
Benchmark field reconstruction, 13-property prediction, multimodal fusion and pairwise cross-modal retrieval.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multimodal fusion improves several prediction tasks over the best unimodal reference, and predicted-density initialization reduces self-consistent-field calculation time by 13.59% on average in paired tests.
infographic.watch_item: Generating reference electronic fields remains computationally costly, and the reported average speedup should not be assumed for every MOF or calculation setup.
infographic.paper_title: MOFFieldBench: A Machine Learning Benchmark for Continuous Electronic Fields in Metal-Organic Frameworks

title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
authors: Yuki K. Wakabayashi, Yui Ogawa
abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM agent rescued failed spectral analyses through bounded fitting adjustments while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic code.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Autonomous exception handling can make self-driving laboratories more robust by recovering defensible measurements and withholding unsupported values.
method: Run a predefined numerical routine to extract Urbach energy from optical transmittance spectra.
Use an LLM agent to assess spectra and fitting diagnostics, accepting valid results unchanged.
Adjust predefined fitting parameters within bounds for recoverable failures; return NaN when evidence is insufficient.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 203 epitaxial β-Ga2O3 film spectra, the agent retained 183 baseline values, recovered 16 of 20 failures, and returned NaN for 4.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covered one material system and analysis workflow; broader reliability remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories

title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
authors: Ilya V. Chepkasov, Alexander V. Shapeev, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

infographic.key_insight: Active learning makes interatomic-potential training more data-efficient by selecting reference calculations relevant to intended simulation conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive training can better align atomistic models with engineering applications spanning alloy mechanics, ion diffusion, functional materials, and reactive systems.
method: Iterate candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating.
Acquire configurations using committee disagreement, Gaussian-process uncertainty, or pretrained-model representations.
Tailor sampling to on-the-fly dynamics, model fine-tuning, or far-from-equilibrium reactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review surveys more than 70 studies, emphasizing 2020–2026, but the abstract reports no pooled quantitative benchmark of accuracy or data savings.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertainty estimates are architecture-dependent and may be least reliable on the unfamiliar configurations where accurate acquisition matters most.
infographic.paper_title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency

title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models
authors: George Nigmatulin, Valentin Mohl, Sascha Frey, Kang Li, Aramis Marti-Shahandeh, Mihai Cucuringu
abstract: Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next-token prediction. We inject execution-style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message-level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order-flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post-execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator-only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square-root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still-short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.

infographic.key_insight: Neural limit order book generators trained only for next-token prediction exhibit emergent market impact, although the observed scaling differs from the traditional square-root law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This financial-market simulation benchmark—not a materials-discovery study—tests whether generative models provide realistic trading environments for agent training.
method: Measure order-flow persistence and price diffusivity during free generation.
Inject execution-style metaorders and compare visible injections with blind simulator-only controls to isolate learned responses.
Estimate impact scaling and amplitude, then measure post-execution relaxation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks found impact exponents of 0.63–1.21, versus the traditional 0.5, with estimators validated on baselines with known dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: No post-execution impact decay was observed in the tested models; short context windows are a tentative explanation, not an established cause.
infographic.paper_title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models

title: Symmetry-Guided Machine Learning of Spin-Dependent Nonlinear Hall Response
authors: Jyotirmoy Sau
abstract: A Berry-curvature dipole can produce a nonlinear Hall current even when the linear Hall response vanishes, but symmetry alone does not determine its magnitude or magnetic tunability. The interplay of structural symmetry, moment orientation, and carrier occupation is examined in a honeycomb model. Curvature maps and the band-summed dipole integrand reveal how velocity and the occupation window near the Fermi level select signed contributions. Removing threefold rotation permits a nonmagnetic dipole perpendicular to the surviving mirror. Generic magnetic reorientation activates the second component and tunes both components through positive and negative values. Global reversal preserves the dipole while reversing the intrinsic linear Hall conductivity, allowing a finite bulk dipole contribution from equally populated reversed domains under uniform-field averaging.A symmetry-constrained polynomial model predicts both dipole components for 256 held-out spin configurations, achieving coefficients of determination $R^2 > 0.9995$ at the reference chemical potential. At fixed carrier density, orientation-dependent shifts of the chemical potential modify the response and yield slightly larger prediction errors for the chosen model. Across the chemical-potential sweep,the prediction accuracy decreases more strongly for $D_y$,revealing an energy dependence of the surrogate's performance. Within semiclassical transport with a constant relaxation time, the calculated dipole determines the angular dependence of the quadratic current and its rectified and second-harmonic components. These results provide a quantitative representation of magnetic-orientation-dependent Berry-curvature dipoles and show how carrier occupation influences both the response and its predictability.

infographic.key_insight: A symmetry-constrained machine-learning model predicts how magnetic orientation tunes the Berry-curvature dipole underlying nonlinear Hall response in a honeycomb model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could guide spin-tunable nonlinear Hall devices whose bulk dipole response survives averaging over equally populated, globally reversed magnetic domains under a uniform field.
method: Analyze symmetry, Berry-curvature maps, and occupation-weighted dipole contributions.
Fit a symmetry-constrained polynomial surrogate for both dipole components.
Evaluate spin configurations, chemical-potential sweeps, and fixed-carrier-density conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: For 256 held-out spin configurations, both predicted dipole components achieved R² > 0.9995 at the reference chemical potential.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on carrier occupation and declines across the chemical-potential sweep, especially for D_y; transport predictions assume a constant relaxation time.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-Guided Machine Learning of Spin-Dependent Nonlinear Hall Response

title: Reaction-induced Localized Annealing for On-chip Materials Discovery
authors: Nensi Toncich, Nerea Abando, Henning Galinski, Frans Spaepen, Ralph Spolenak
abstract: On-chip thermal processing is a key technology for materials discovery across all disciplines of the natural sciences. Here, we present a microfabricated heat-delivery platform that enables reaction-induced localized on-chip annealing up to 1400°C. A buried reactive multilayer combined with a nanometric diffusion barrier provide ultra-fast heating and quenching rates on the order of 10$^6$°C s$^{-1}$ as illustrated by the generation of ultra-high aspect ratio microstructures during rapid-solidification and the stabilization of dopant-free tetragonal zirconia at room temperature. Rapid kinetics also enable the observation of transient states of capillary-driven hole collapse in melts. Our work expands localized high-temperature processing routes and offers a material-independent approach for rapid screening of multidimensional nanomaterials on and off-equilibrium.

infographic.key_insight: A microfabricated reactive multilayer platform enables localized on-chip annealing up to 1400°C for rapid materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Localized, ultrafast thermal processing could accelerate screening of nanomaterials and access nonequilibrium structures and phases.
method: Use a buried reactive multilayer as a localized heat source.
Combine it with a nanometric diffusion barrier.
Apply rapid heating and quenching to probe solidification, phase stabilization, and melt dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports heating and quenching rates on the order of 10^6°C/s, ultra-high-aspect-ratio microstructures, dopant-free tetragonal zirconia retained at room temperature, and transient stages of capillary-driven hole collapse in melts.
infographic.watch_item: Thermal uniformity, process reproducibility, and compatibility across material systems require validation beyond the demonstrations described in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Reaction-induced Localized Annealing for On-chip Materials Discovery

title: Stabilization of Ferroelectric Domains via Interfacial Strain in HoFeO3- BaTiO3 Nanofiber Heterostructures for Enhanced Hybrid Energy Harvesting
authors: Smita Chaturvedi, Swathi Krishna, Shivshankar Jokare, Supriya Sahoo, Vikash Kushwaha, Priyank Shyam
abstract: Piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are an attractive platform for self-powered mechanical-energy harvesting, but their output is often limited by depolarization fields, charge leakage, and inefficient stress transfer to the active dipoles, particularly in polymer-dominated composites. Here we report HoFeO3-BaTiO3 (HFO-BTO) nanofiber heterostructures prepared by alternating sol-gel electrospinning, in which orthorhombic HoFeO3 (Pbnm) and tetragonal BaTiO3 (P4mm) coexist in intimate contact. Rietveld-refined X-ray diffraction, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy indicate interfacial lattice distortion. Polarization-electric field loops show that the heterostructure retains a polarization comparable to that of BaTiO3 (16.39 vs 15.80 microcoulombs per square centimeter at zero field) while its switching-current maximum moves to a higher field (about 7 vs about 3.5 kilovolts per centimeter), consistent with strain-stabilized ferroelectric domains. When the nanofibers are encapsulated in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and excited under cyclic impact, the device produces a hybrid output: the piezoelectric response of the strained BaTiO3 is supplemented by a triboelectric contribution from contact electrification. The HFO-BTO device delivers open-circuit voltage peaks of about +6 volts and -8 volts and a power density of 24.31 microwatts per cubic centimeter at a 4.7 megaohm load. This is 2.4 times the value for an identically fabricated BaTiO3 device (10.00 microwatts per cubic centimeter) and 8.7 times that of the HoFeO3 device (2.78 microwatts per cubic centimeter). These results link interface-driven lattice distortion to improved electromechanical output and identify all-oxide nanofiber heterostructures as a promising route to lead-free energy harvesting.

infographic.key_insight: Interfacial lattice distortion in HoFeO3–BaTiO3 nanofibers is consistent with stabilized ferroelectric domains and enhanced hybrid energy harvesting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lead-free oxide nanofiber heterostructures offer a route to improve mechanical-energy harvesting in flexible PDMS-encapsulated devices.
method: Fabricate HoFeO3–BaTiO3 heterostructures by alternating sol–gel electrospinning.
Probe crystal structure and interfaces using Rietveld-refined XRD, high-resolution TEM, and Raman spectroscopy.
Measure polarization switching and cyclic-impact energy harvesting against single-oxide controls.
infographic.evidence_signal: The heterostructure retained polarization comparable to BaTiO3 (16.39 vs 15.80 µC/cm² at zero field) and delivered 24.31 µW/cm³ at 4.7 MΩ, outperforming BaTiO3 and HoFeO3 controls by 2.4× and 8.7×.
infographic.watch_item: The reported output combines piezoelectric and triboelectric contributions, so their separate roles require quantification.
infographic.paper_title: Stabilization of Ferroelectric Domains via Interfacial Strain in HoFeO3- BaTiO3 Nanofiber Heterostructures for Enhanced Hybrid Energy Harvesting

title: Learning the Geometry of Materials Space with Trained Neural Tangent Kernels
authors: Daniel Kaplan, Gabriel Kotliar, Anirvan M Sengupta
abstract: Neural networks trained to predict materials properties learn representations whose physical content can be difficult to extract. We use the neural tangent kernel (NTK), evaluated at trained parameters, to recover the geometry learned by a network that predicts superconducting transition temperatures from elemental composition alone. Kernel ridge regression with the trained NTK closely reproduces the network's predictive performance and substantially outperforms regression with the initial kernel. Spectral analysis and multidimensional scaling reveal a geometry dominated by a small number of directions. Clustering and local neighborhood analysis organize compounds into recognizable superconducting families and connect materials with related chemical and correlated-electron properties despite substantial differences in $T_c$. These results establish trained tangent kernels as practical probes of learned materials representations, connecting property prediction with the exploration of materials space.

infographic.key_insight: Trained neural tangent kernels expose a low-dimensional geometry that groups superconductors into recognizable families beyond similarities in transition temperature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can help researchers inspect composition-based property predictors and explore chemically related materials.
method: Train a neural network to predict superconducting transition temperature from elemental composition.
Evaluate its neural tangent kernel at trained parameters and use it for kernel ridge regression.
Analyze the learned geometry with spectral analysis, multidimensional scaling, clustering, and local neighborhoods.
infographic.evidence_signal: Kernel ridge regression with the trained kernel closely reproduces the network’s predictive performance and substantially outperforms regression with the initial kernel.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports results for superconducting transition temperatures but does not establish generalization to other materials properties.
infographic.paper_title: Learning the Geometry of Materials Space with Trained Neural Tangent Kernels

title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
authors: Akash Gupta, Austin Guo, Jie Deng
abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.

infographic.key_insight: Ammonia and hydrogen can separate under Uranus- and Neptune-like conditions, while remaining fully miscible in warmer sub-Neptune envelopes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The predicted phase boundaries can improve planetary interior models by constraining ammonia rainout and its effects on composition, heat transport and structure.
method: Train machine-learning interatomic potentials on density functional theory calculations.
Run large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations across 500–4000 K and 0.1–100 GPa.
Map coexisting phase compositions and the critical curve separating miscibility from phase separation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The critical temperature rises from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to about 2000 K near 30 GPa, with no phase separation found at 3000 or 4000 K up to 100 GPa.
infographic.watch_item: Ammonia rainout is inferred from comparison with published planetary thermal profiles rather than directly observed.
infographic.paper_title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics

title: Atomic-level study of dose-dependent lattice thermal conductivity degradation in irradiated tungsten
authors: Mary K Chessey, José Julio Gutiérrez Moreno, Sajjan Singh Mehta, Paolo Settembri, Arda Erbasan, Dominik Freinberger
abstract: Plasma-facing components (PFCs) in future fusion reactors must withstand extreme environments, making tungsten (W) a prime candidate material due to its high thermal conductivity, high melting temperature, low sputtering yield, low tritium absorption. However, neutron irradiation introduces complex nanostructural defects that severely degrade these critical properties. In this work, we use Non-Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics (NEMD) simulations coupled with the Creation Relaxation Algorithm (CRA) to investigate the lattice thermal conductivity (kappa) of W across a wide range of irradiation doses. Systems treated with different doses up to 1.8 canonical displacements per atom (cdpa) were simulated to generate and study diverse defect structures, including vacancies and self-interstitial atom (SIA) clusters. By correlating spatially-resolved temperature gradients with local defect concentrations, we show that even small changes in defect type and distribution significantly affect thermal transport. We employ Machine Learning (ML) models to develop a quantitative relationship between the defect features and the resulting thermal conductivity degradation. The ML analysis identifies vacancy density as the dominant structural factor controlling thermal transport. We found a significant, nonlinear suppression of kappa with increasing defect density. Predictive multi-defect mapping built upon our ML model resolved a step-like degradation transition at a critical vacancy threshold of 0.05 at.%, beyond which phonon scattering completely saturated and capped the maximum relative lattice thermal conductivity degradation at approximately 30 at.%. This integrated simulation and ML approach provides a powerful, predictive framework for quantifying the complex relationship between structure and thermal conductivity in irradiated fusion materials.

infographic.key_insight: Vacancy density dominates the predicted degradation of tungsten’s lattice thermal conductivity, with a step-like transition near 0.05 at.% vacancies followed by saturation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Defect-based conductivity predictions could help assess irradiation-induced heat-removal losses in tungsten plasma-facing components for fusion reactors.
method: Generate irradiation defects using the Creation Relaxation Algorithm.
Use non-equilibrium molecular dynamics to relate local temperature gradients to defect concentrations.
Train machine-learning models to map defect features to lattice thermal conductivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations spanning irradiation doses up to 1.8 canonical displacements per atom show nonlinear, saturating conductivity degradation, with machine learning identifying vacancy density as the dominant structural factor.
infographic.watch_item: The study addresses lattice conductivity; assessing total heat transport in reactor tungsten also requires electronic contributions and experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Atomic-level study of dose-dependent lattice thermal conductivity degradation in irradiated tungsten

title: Early-stage local melting during solid-state sintering of a Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf alloy: A combined thermodynamic and kinetic analysis
authors: Andrea Skolakova, Hana Lesakova, Frantisek Lukac, Marketa Jarosova, Jan Pinc
abstract: Complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) combining elements from 3d transition and refractory groups, specifically Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf-based shape memory systems, exhibit excellent functional properties but present significant manufacturing challenges via powder metallurgy. In this study, a non-equimolar Cu15Ni35Ti25Zr12.5Hf12.5 (at. %) alloy was successfully produced by induction melting, followed by atomization and subsequent consolidation via Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at temperatures ranging from 850 to 1100 C. Although global equilibrium phase diagrams predict solid-state stability up to 1260 C, localized melting unexpectedly occurred during SPS at 1100 C. By combining retrospective Scheil-Gulliver solidification simulations with 2D local equilibrium heat maps, we demonstrate that this early-stage melting is not driven by macroscopic thermal gradients, but by microsegregation inherited from atomization. During solid-state heating, thermally activated short-range diffusion, accelerated by high defect densities at particle interfaces, partitions Ti towards the interparticle network, leaving Cu-enriched regions (up to ~41 at. %) within the particle interiors. Owing to the strongly negative mixing enthalpy of Cu with Hf (-19.2 kJ/mol for $ΔH_{mix}^{l-l}$) and, to a lesser extent, with Ti, the local solidus of these Cu-rich regions is dramatically depressed. Upon heating to 1100 C, these regions cross their local solidus and form a liquid phase, whose solidification produces the Cu-Hf co-segregation. This framework accounts for localized melting phenomena in rapidly solidified CCA powders containing low-melting constituents with strong negative mixing enthalpies.

infographic.key_insight: Inherited microsegregation and short-range diffusion create Cu-rich regions that melt locally at 1100 °C, below the alloy’s predicted global solid-state stability limit of 1260 °C.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPS processing windows for Cu–Ni–Ti–Zr–Hf powders should account for local composition-dependent solidus temperatures, not just bulk equilibrium predictions.
method: Induction melting and atomization of Cu15Ni35Ti25Zr12.5Hf12.5, followed by SPS at 850–1100 °C.
Retrospective Scheil–Gulliver solidification simulations.
2D local-equilibrium heat maps to assess segregation-driven melting.
infographic.evidence_signal: Localized melting at 1100 °C, Cu enrichment up to approximately 41 at. %, and Cu–Hf co-segregation after solidification support the proposed mechanism.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify diffusion kinetics or validate the mechanism beyond this alloy and processing range.
infographic.paper_title: Early-stage local melting during solid-state sintering of a Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf alloy: A combined thermodynamic and kinetic analysis

title: SIESTA-QCOMP: Bridging Classical and Quantum Computing for Strongly Correlated Systems
authors: Yann Pouillon, Federico Marchesin, Ivano Tavernelli, Emilio Artacho
abstract: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the established workhorse of computational materials science, yet it faces fundamental challenges with strongly correlated electrons, such as in transition metal complexes and bond-breaking processes. While quantum computing offers a theoretically exact path to resolve these problems, current hardware limitations prohibit fully quantum simulations of realistic material systems. To bridge this gap, we present SIESTA-QCOMP, a modular suite embedding quantum methodologies within DFT. Harnessing SIESTA's localised basis set, we implement a projection-based embedding scheme that treats the bulk environment classically while mapping the strongly correlated "impurity" subspace to a quantum processor. The architecture uses a socket-based driver to orchestrate workflows between the Fortran-based SIESTA engine and Python-based frameworks like Qiskit, ensuring high interoperability. We detail the hybrid workflow, currently utilising a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and discuss the road map toward methods such as Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD). We illustrate the framework on an hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation and argue that such hybrid architectures are not merely interim solutions but essential foundations for integrating quantum utility into materials design, as envisioned by our broader QCOMP4DFT initiative.

infographic.key_insight: SIESTA-QCOMP embeds a quantum-treated, strongly correlated subspace within a classical DFT environment to target material systems beyond current fully quantum simulation capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The modular architecture connects SIESTA with quantum software frameworks, providing a route toward hybrid simulations relevant to materials design.
method: Use SIESTA’s localised basis for projection-based partitioning of the classical environment and correlated impurity.
Treat the impurity with a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE).
Coordinate Fortran-based SIESTA and Python frameworks such as Qiskit through a socket-based driver.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract illustrates the framework with a hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation but reports no quantitative accuracy, runtime, or hardware benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Current quantum hardware limits practical simulations, and Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD) remains a roadmap method rather than a demonstrated capability.
infographic.paper_title: SIESTA-QCOMP: Bridging Classical and Quantum Computing for Strongly Correlated Systems
